claims.text: The as-cast CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a uniform microstructure.
Friction-induced oxidation forms a dynamic tribo-oxide film during sliding tribo-corrosion of CoCrFeMnNi.
The tribo-oxide film is self-healing and mechanically robust.
Ambient oxygen availability governs formation of the tribo-oxide film.
The tribo-oxide film passivates the alloy surface.
In oxygen-rich conditions, the tribo-oxide film limits metal dissolution.
In oxygen-rich conditions, the tribo-oxide film reduces mechanical wear by acting as a protective barrier.
Reduced oxygen availability produces insufficient or compromised tribo-oxide film formation.
Insufficient film formation exposes the metal surface and increases corrosion.
Insufficient film formation exposes the metal surface and increases wear.
Argon saturation suppresses tribo-oxide film formation.
Relative to an argon-saturated baseline, oxygen-rich testing will lower total degradation.
Relative to an argon-saturated baseline, oxygen-rich testing will lower metal dissolution rates.
Relative to an argon-saturated baseline, oxygen-rich testing will lower wear-track depth or volume loss.
The protective effect should hold at moderate sliding speeds and loads because oxide-film rupture is minimal.
At extreme mechanical conditions, the film may be disrupted regardless of oxygen availability and lose its protective effect.
The proposed controlled comparison varies oxygen availability while holding mechanical loading and other test conditions constant.
The general role of tribo-oxide films in reducing wear and corrosion is supported by prior work.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents one oxide film as a common mediator that simultaneously lowers wear and corrosion, and predicts that both components change in the same direction, but the predicted-outcome field calls this a 'decoupling' of the protective effects. The stated outcomes instead describe coupled co-variation.
